statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more stroke, most clearly with bleeding into the brain (intracerebral haemorrhage), and the Chinese study found no sign of a lower risk at low intake; cohort studies comparing people who drink with people who do not found no overall difference in stroke but more strokes at higher intakes. No paper read gives absolute risks of stroke by amount. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults from ten areas, followed about 10 years, men's stroke risk rose steadily across six groups whose genotypes and area predicted mean intakes of 4 to 256 g of ethanol a week: per 100 g a week (about 14 g a day, editors' arithmetic) ischaemic stroke 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24; 2,790 cases) and all stroke 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); the lowest group, in which two thirds did not drink, showed no sign of a raised risk, and the next two groups (about 100 g a week) had higher, not lower, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage than the three lowest groups pooled (about 25 g a week); the same genotypes showed no association in women, few of whom drink (ischaemic stroke 0.98, 0.88 to 1.09; intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96, 0.82 to 1.12); and self-reported drinking in the same men showed a U shape, with lower stroke risk at about 100 g a week than in non-drinkers and former drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, those authors estimate that alcohol caused about 8 in 100 ischaemic strokes and 16 in 100 intracerebral haemorrhages among the men studied (a model estimate). In European-descent summary data the odds of stroke were 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45) per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week, 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32) (Larsson et al., 2020); in UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder gave 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54), not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of ischaemic stroke in the studies with subtype data (0.83, 0.72 to 0.95) but no difference in all stroke (0.98, 0.90 to 1.07; 10,164 strokes) (Holmes et al., 2014). In cohort studies, people who drank had, against non-drinkers (most groups including former drinkers), no different risk of new stroke (0.98, 0.91 to 1.06; 17 studies) or of stroke death (1.06, 0.91 to 1.23; 10 studies), and against lifetime abstainers a higher risk of stroke death (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53; 3 studies); by intake, new strokes were less common at up to 14.9 g a day (0.81 and 0.80; 3 studies each) and more common above 60 g a day (1.62, 1.32 to 1.98; 4 studies) (Ronksley et al., 2011); in the GBD 2016 curves ischaemic stroke dipped at low intake without statistical significance. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and the risk rose steadily with the amount, with no dip at low amounts. Strokes caused by bleeding in the brain rose the most. Women, few of whom drink, showed no link with the same genes. Gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction. Older studies that compared people who drink with people who don't found no overall difference in stroke, slightly fewer strokes at low amounts in a few studies, and more at high amounts. None of these studies says how many extra strokes this means out of 100.
population: Men in the China Kadoorie Biobank (161,498 genotyped adults from ten areas; women as a check); people of European descent in genome-wide consortia and UK Biobank (Larsson et al.; Biddinger et al.) and in 56 pooled studies (Holmes et al.); adults in prospective cohorts to 2009 (Ronksley et al.); the studies behind the GBD 2016 curves
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake (ALDH2 and ADH1B genotypes with area, as six groups of mean male intake from 4 to 256 g/week; up to 94 variants for log drinks a week; a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder; the ADH1B rs1229984 variant), and self-reported intake in grams of ethanol a day in cohorts
comparator: Lower genetically predicted intake (per 100 or 280 g/week against the lowest group; per standard deviation; non-carriers); in cohorts, non-drinkers as each study defined them (mostly including former drinkers), and lifetime abstainers in a subset
outcome: Stroke: ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, subarachnoid haemorrhage (one dataset) and all stroke; new strokes and stroke deaths
magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; genetic, per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake): ischaemic stroke RR 1.27 (1.13–1.43; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36–1.84; 2,790), all stroke 1.38 (1.26–1.51; 9,189); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04–1.14), 1.18 (1.12–1.24), 1.12 (1.09–1.16); single variants (GG against AG) stroke 1.19 (1.13–1.24) rs671 and 1.19 (1.11–1.27) rs1229984; women ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88–1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82–1.12); conventional, current drinkers per 280 g/week, 1.28 (1.19–1.38), 1.59 (1.37–1.85), 1.35 (1.27–1.44), with a U shape against non-drinkers (not printed); attributable shares if there is no protection and the relation is log-linear: about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men. Larsson et al. 2020 (per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week): stroke OR 1.27 (1.12–1.45), adjusted for smoking liability 1.21 (1.05–1.40); ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09–1.46); intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70–7.32); subarachnoid haemorrhage (UK Biobank) 2.47 (1.08–5.62); ADH1B variant alone ischaemic stroke 1.31 (1.05–1.65), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31–101.46). Biddinger et al. 2022: stroke 1.26 (1.04–1.54; P = .021, threshold P < .008). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering variant): all stroke 0.98 (0.90–1.07), ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72–0.95). Ronksley et al. 2011 (cohorts; against non-drinkers, mostly current): incident stroke 0.98 (0.91–1.06), stroke death 1.06 (0.91–1.23); against lifetime abstainers 0.93 (0.85–1.02) and 1.29 (1.09–1.53); incident stroke by intake (under 2.5 to over 60 g/day) 0.81, 0.80, 0.92, 1.15, 1.62 (1.32–1.98); haemorrhagic 1.14 (0.97–1.34), ischaemic 0.92 (0.85–1.00). No absolute risks in any paper read.

risk_of_bias.note: Rated for the genetic association. The genetic design protects against confounding by lifestyle and against illness changing drinking, and here the remaining threats were tested without removing the association: in China, women, in whom the same genotypes barely change drinking, showed no stroke association (a check for paths outside alcohol), the instrument was very strong and comparisons were within area; in European data the estimate fell only from 1.27 to 1.21 after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, never-smokers gave similar results, and the ADH1B variant alone, which did not predict smoking, gave 1.31 for ischaemic stroke. Paths that remain possible (acetaldehyde exposure per drink with ALDH2, education with ADH1B, UK Biobank in both exposure and outcome data, prevalent cases in the ADH1B study) are judged unlikely to change the direction, so the editors do not rate down. The cohort figures (comparison groups with former drinkers) are given as context and rated in the answer on heart disease.

inconsistency.note: The genetic studies agree in direction for ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage; the ADH1B study's null result for all stroke (0.98) rests on fewer strokes and a smaller difference in intake, which its authors call a limitation, and its ischaemic-stroke subset agrees. The cohort dip at low intake, against its absence in the Chinese genetic analysis, is the reference-group question of the cohort studies and is stated rather than rated.

indirectness.note: Chinese men drinking mainly spirits and European-descent populations; the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted log drinks a week and cannot be put into grams; women only as a check in China. Stated, not rated.

imprecision.note: The main genetic intervals exclude no difference; the European intracerebral haemorrhage interval is wide (1.70 to 7.32).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with four genetic studies.

large_effect.note: Per 100 g a week the relative risks are 1.09 to 1.18; not large.

dose_response.note: Risk rose steadily across the six genetic groups in China and, in cohorts, from about 15 g to more than 60 g a day. Not upgraded: the Chinese gradient is the slope estimate itself, fitted through six group means of self-reported intake, and pleiotropy cannot be wholly excluded; with this upgrade the rating would be moderate.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief). The design addresses confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation, and its main remaining weaknesses were tested here (a check in women, allowance for genetic liability to smoking, never-smokers, a single-variant analysis), so the editors do not rate down for confounding or risk of bias; this is logged for the senior author under the round's rule. What the design cannot show is the size of the effect in grams in European data and the curve at the lowest intakes outside the Chinese study. No downgrade and no upgrade: low. Status replicated: two independent genetic studies in different ancestries (Millwood et al.; Larsson et al.) agree, Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank, overlapping Larsson et al.'s outcome data) points the same way, and the ADH1B study agrees for ischaemic stroke; Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. share two authors. The cohort results (Ronksley et al.) and the GBD 2016 curves describe the conventional association and are not counted as replication of the genetic finding.
